Resgo still has no UI, but before I start developing it I have one more feature to build:

Portfolio simulation.

Portfolio simulation is the Resgo end-game. Resgo already provides a very performant Prospect level simulation engine, from subsurface through to commercial metrics, and that leaves it well positioned for zooming out one more level to portfolio level analysis.

My goals at the outset are the following:

  1. Allow grouping Prospects into Portfolios, with lossless representation
  2. Represent parent-child relationships between Prospects to allow for dependency propagation
  3. Dependency propagation should allows information to flow between prospects and their children, so that drilling outcomes follow logical chains during simulation
  4. Use those logical chains to derive stand-alone and full-cycle metrics for decision gating
  5. Report accepted, strategic (full cycle economics says drill) and rejected prospect decisions at the portfolio level

Structure and constraints

The most convenient representation of a Portfolio with these constraints in mind is a tree. Prospects can have children: opportunities who’s risks are affected by outcomes in their parent. That creates some limitations (sibling Prospects can’t have dependencies) but I think the simplicity of tree depth traversal, and limiting onerous dependency configuration, will make that trade-off worthwhile.

For lossless Prospect representation in Resgo, this means that dependency must be represented at the reservoir and risk factor level. This is a complication that I believe will pay dividends in granular configuration and interpretability of portfolio simulations, matching the mental models in subsurface teams’ heads when defining dependencies between opportunitities.

It will mean, for example, that reservoirs in the Propects tree can share strong P(charge) dependency. If the parent fails on charge, that heavily impacts the P(charge) of children. This is well suited for modelling play-openers on untested migration pathways, for example. Similarly these dependencies can be captured for reservoir presence for testing sand fairways, and seal/trap for things like demonstrating fault seal.

Dependency mechanics

I’m going to bring up Bayes again, sorry1.

Dependency in this framing is a Bayesian probability update from the prior risk probability (say a 0.5 probability of charge in the child reservoir). Mechanically, the update is applied in odds space:

\[ O_{\mathrm{post}} = O_{\mathrm{prior}} \times \text{LH} \]

or, equivalently, in log-odds space:

\[ \ln_2\left(O_{\mathrm{post}}\right) = \ln_2\left(O_{\mathrm{prior}}\right) + \ln_2\left(\text{LH}\right) \]

where \(O = p / (1 - p)\) is the odds, \(\text{LH}\) is the likelihood ratio, and \(\ln_2\) denotes a base-2 logarithm.

Using a base-2 logarithm means that the evidence term, \(\ln_2(\text{LH})\), is measured in bits: positive bits increase the odds of success, negative bits decrease them, and zero bits leave the prior odds unchanged.

You’ll have to humor me because it seems weird, but this is a very mentally ergonomic way of framing Bayesian probability updates.

Starting from a prior probability of 0.50 as an example, each additional bit doubles the likelihood ratio:

Evidence Likelihood ratio Posterior probability
-4 bits 1:16 0.06
-3 bits 1:8 0.11
-2 bits 1:4 0.20
-1 bit 1:2 0.33
0 bits 1:1 0.50
1 bit 2:1 0.67
2 bits 4:1 0.80
3 bits 8:1 0.89
4 bits 16:1 0.94

Operating in this way means that updates are commutative: you can add and subtract bits of evidence to arrive at a final posterior. This is mental Bayes trickery, but is also useful for efficient and interpretable communication of risk dependencies in the context of the portfolio simulator.

“If the Bonanza prospect fails on charge, how bad would that be for charge risk at Buffet?”

“They’re on the same migration corridor so really bad… probably -4 bits.”

“We did see shows on that separate migration corridor connecting to Buffet though, remember?”

“Fair enough, that’s probably worth 1 bit. -3 bits total then.”

Now, regardless of P(charge) at Bonanza, the information it provides to Buffet is explicitly communicated.

If, for example, P(charge) is 0.5 across prospects and Bonanza fails on charge, that means Buffet gets a P(charge) of 0.11 (killing it). If Bonanza is charged though, that increase P(charge) at Buffet to 0.89!

See? We can all become Bayesians with some language tricks.

There is a technical wrinkle that positive and negative updates are not necessarily symmetric (relevant example here), so the code should make that explicit, but default to symmetric updates.

Decision Gates

For the portfolio simulation to be coherent, decisions need to be made about whether to drill for each Prospect, based on the information available. That requires point estimate hurdles. Decisions aren’t made stochastically. We can’t just use the simulation result to determine the right path on every iteration, because the decision maker doesn’t know what will happen. That means a decision criterion needs to be specified.

This can be things like a positive risked mean NPV (equivalent to EMV):

\[ \mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{NPV}_{\mathrm{risked}}\right] > 0 \]

or a positive risked 90th percentile NPV:

\[ Q_{0.10}\left(\mathrm{NPV}_{\mathrm{risked}}\right) > 0 \]

But it needs to be agreed upon up front for the portfolio simulation to operate. Most companies have defined hurdles like this in place, but there may be situations where hurdles are prospect specific.

Luckily, because Resgo simulates everything in a single integrated chain, these decision metrics will be consistently applied to rigorously defined stochastic ranges of NPV. That is a rare luxury in portfolio analysis contexts.

Simulation process

Resgo allows us to very ergonomically simulate the entire portfolio tree in a forward pass, adjusting risk factors on success/failure case of parent nodes, then run the decision gating logic on the results to determine which prospects get drilled and which get rejected. We can then aggregate the portfolio level NPV to assess its overall economic value and uncertainty.

Additional wrinkles

Because we are simulating an ensemble of prospects, we need to be careful to define a few things up front.

We need a single price deck, especially if it is stochastic, to avoid individual prospects getting their own price histories.

We also need a single economic basis for escalation and discounting. That means every prospect has NPV calculations consistent on a single “start date” for the whole portfolio. Failing to do this would unfairly inflate the value of future prospects in the schedule.

Strategic value

Something compelling that this gives us is the ability to quantify the strategic value of prospects. This is the stand-alone value of the prospect, plus any downstream opportunity it creates.

This means that a stand-alone prospect with negative NPV—maybe due to a low P(Success)—can have its downstream value quantified and summed to make it full-cycle economic, even if it is not drillable on its own merits.

For example:

Hear me out.

Boring is a high risk, low return prospect. It will probably fail, and it’s a small closure. It’s a dog.

But if Buffet is successful, you’d be crazy not to drill it.

This is the crazy senior geologist speaking. He has a mad twinkle in his eye, and he knows nobody will listen, but he knows he is right, dammit.

Why is he right?

Because the information that Boring provides, expensive as it may be, has huge upside.

A success at Boring would boost the P(success) of Bonanza, a high risk, high reward prospect that nobody is considering because “there is no migration that way”. Bonanza is a play opener, it has several follow-ups, all of which are currently high risk, but high value.

So you drill Boring to open up the play.

I’ve been the crazy guy before. I’ve never been able to quantify any of this stuff persuasively. Resgo lets me quantify the whole lot, all the way through to economics. It becomes a simple matter of well applied decision theory, a consequence of your decision metrics, and the risks and uncertainties in your portfolio.

Resgo tells you to do it.

And the tool isn’t crazy! It’s just uncertainty propagation, Bayesian updating and economics. Don’t argue with the results, just make sure you verify your inputs.

Now let’s try to do it.

High risk

You’ll notice this whole portfolio looks very high risk. That is because all risk factors are being applied with our current state of information. The entire portfolio has high charge risk, a P(Charge) of 0.4 for Buffet, Bitesize, Budget and Boring, and an even harsher 0.2 for Bonanza and its children, making them all a bad bet. This is an untested migration pathway in our basin.

The opportunities don’t necessarily hold up on their own merits. That is why strategic value is so important. Strategic, full-cycle value of these prospects will be simulated on a portfolio basis.

Portfolio model

The portfolio manages all these prospects, along with their parent-child relationships and information sharing for risk factors. For simplicity we will just model information sharing for P(charge), but a user could model relationships between reservoir risk factors as they see fit.

The Resgo Portfolio, as it turns out, is quite a complicated object to visualize. Every node in the tree is stochastic, and outcomes are being bifurcated via the information sharing between nodes. That creates a difficult to interpret cash flow plot:

Portfolio mean case

This change will result in the following ValueError: cannot be aligned with join='exact' because index/labels/sizes are not equal along these coordinates (dimensions): 'Date' ('Date',) The recommendation is to set join explicitly for this case.

This might be (and I’m really not sure yet) the best way to visualize the portfolio value through time. I say I’m not sure because taking the mean across the whole simulated array by month is smoothing through a lot of complexity. I can’t stack prospects while also visualizing uncertainty, so a mean timeline is a good compromise, even though the mean case is not actually a case, it never appears in the simulated array.

I could use the P50 (median) case, but then the problem becomes what we actually mean by P50, at this level of analysis. I can’t take the P50 array of each individual prospect, because outcomes are being bifurcated by information flowing from parent to child, making a median of limited interest, and that P50 outcome at each prospect never appears in the array as a case, either.

Some brainstorming and refinement will be needed here, I think.

It’s pretty cool though.

You’ll notice that the decision assigned to Boring in the table above is strategic. That is because Boring was not drillable on its own merits, it had negative EMV. Considering its downstream opportunity creation, however, made it a clear decision to drill.

The other prospect that looked questionable on a first pass, Budget, was rejected in the portfolio. If Budget opened up downstream opportunity, it would likely be set to strategic as well.

Overall impression

The first thing that jumps out is that the commercial outcomes at the portfolio aggregated level are extremely uncertain. This makes sense, if you think about it. We don’t even know if this corridor is charged. That means we have anything between zero opportunity here, and potentially 8 decently sized prospects. That is going to be a very wide range.

To illustrate this uncertainty a bit more:

If Buffet fails, the entire portfolio is ruled out. Too risky on charge.

If Buffet succeeds, that boosts the P(Charge) of its children Bitesize, Budget, and Boring. That doesn’t mean they all succeed (other risk factors are at play) but they become much more likely to.

If Boring is charged, that information flows to Bonanza and its children. These prospects were written off as extremely high risk before drilling with P(Charge) of 0.2. The success upstream at Budget, even though Budget on its own is sub-economic, opens up the Bonanza play. That has huge strategic value, as Bonanza is the biggest prospect in the portfolio on an unrisked basis.

Because of the dependencies between prospects in the portfolio, standalone economic metrics aren’t really enough to communicate value. Most of the value in Buffet is not standalone, it is in the downstream information it provides to child prospects, connected via the P(Charge) dependency.

Similarly, Boring would never get drilled on its own merits, it provides value via its downstream consequences. These complicated arguments are very difficult to make in normal circumstances, especially under uncertainty. This is my best attempt at making the whole simulated system explicit.
